newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel clarifies shekel trading band changes.
newsitem.headline: Israel clarifies shekel trading band changes.

text.p: The foreign exchange reform approved by Israel's cabinet on Wednesday widens the shekel's total trading band to 28 percent from 14 percent, central bank officials explained.
Until now the shekel, pegged to a basket of foreign currencies, was allowed to fluctuate in a range of seven percent above or below a diagonal designed to devalue the shekel by six percent a year.
Under the new plan, the lower band remains the same while the upper band rises to 21 percent. The spread between the top and bottom band, therefore, will be 28 percent.
At the same time, the upper slope will continue on a six percent incline over the course of a year while the bottom slope will rise at a rate of only four percent.
This means the total band will widen by two percent so. By the end of the year the spread between the upper and lower band will be 30 percent.
This achieves the goal of the Bank of Israel's proposal to widen both bands to 15 percent.

Since high interest rates have buoyed the shekel, the currency basket's exchange rate has hovered on the bottom band for most of the past year. This has forced the central bank to intervene massively, buying dollars to prevent the shekel from appreciating beyond the trading band.
The Bank of Israel had pushed for a widening of the band to give it relief from having to intervene constantly in the market.

Even though the bottom band was not expanded, the reforms allow the central bank to be less involved in the market. If the basket exchange rate continues to sit on the bottom band, the central bank will still have to intervene less because at the bottom band it is committed to only a four percent devaluation of the shekel instead of six percent.

Under the new plan, at the end of a year both bands will slope at the same rate. The new rate, as yet undecided, will reflect the difference between Israel's inflation and that of its major trading partners.
Israel's inflation last year totalled 10.6 percent. Economists estimate inflation this year at 8.5-9.0 percent.
